doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Learning film scoring and Victor Young facing Cecil B. DeMille
summary: He learned scoring by watching; story of DeMille demanding melody from Victor Young's main title.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: What is it, “One O’clock Jump” is like in D flat or something. I always wondered why — that’s pushing it. The process of learning to do scoring for film, how did you learn to do that, with a click track and all that kind of thing?

I think again by brute force. If you sit there — I sat in the orchestra and watched guys die in front of producers. Good composers. One: Aaron Copland — die in front of these, forgive me, idiot producers who want everything to sound like Wagner or something. I mean that’s the only name they knew you know. They didn’t know Mahler or Bruckner then. Everything was Vaagner—Vaagner—Vaagner. And I think sitting behind the piano bench or sitting behind the piano looking and watching was almost the best teacher. Also, we lived in a very cruel society at that time because what I observed I suffered under when I tried to step forward. There wasn’t any subtlety. If things didn’t work it didn’t work and you were out the door. I mean I watched men like Victor Young, I’ll never forget, we played a main title for Cecil B. DeMille and Victor was a magnificent orchestrator and I mean the Paramount Orchestra was first class. And there were two pianos, I was on the date. And we played this main title we just absolutely were in awe of his skill of putting it together. And Cecil B. came in in his pates and his entourage following him and sat down. Now we sit in this grim, soundproof studio. We play this magnificent main title and there’s quietude because you never spoke until the boss spoke you know. And Mr. DeMille said something like, “That isn’t my music, is it? Is that the music you wrote? Is that the music for this film?” He said, “Well if it is I don’t hear any melody.” So there was kind of a deathly silence, DeMille and his entourage left, and he said, “I’ll be back in a week or so, but I want to hear some melody.” So a week later he came back and Victor as a jazztet scored the melody in unison for the whole orchestra.
But he didn’t get the joke, he didn’t get the joke, so it was no joke. But I thought of living through those things, and it was a very tough, very tough business.
